# corpus


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Training the learned scorer needs labeled text, and no human has labeled
any. This module builds the corpus by weak supervision: the rules pick
confident slop from my own reply history, human-authored sources supply
the clean side, and the ambiguous middle joins neither. The one
human-labeled set, replies that drew a complaint in a session, is
written separately and reserved for evaluation. Rows carry their source,
so any experiment can slice, reweight, or hold out a source later.

``` python
from fastcore.test import *
```

## The label-side scorer

The rules select the positives, and the forest’s features must stay
independent of that selection. Most features are safe by construction:
burstiness, sentence lengths, part-of-speech rates, specifics density,
and the referential measures share no vocabulary with any rule. The
connective rates do: `furthermore` sits in both the connective sets and
the filler-transitions lexicon. A word in both places would let the
label leak into a feature.
[`label_overlap`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#label_overlap)
computes the shared words mechanically, and
[`label_density`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#label_density)
scores with findings on those words dropped. The labels come from
[`label_density`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#label_density);
users keep
[`score_text`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/score.html#score_text)
unchanged.

## Replies from the session mirror

`llmsurgery` keeps an ipynb mirror of every session on the machine. Each
prompt message carries its reply, and a reply mixes mid-turn notes, tool
blocks, and the final message. The user only reacts to the final
message, and the labels must attach to what the user read.
[`reply_final`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#reply_final)
therefore keeps the text after the last tool block and drops the rest.
[`mirror_replies`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#mirror_replies)
walks recent mirrors and yields one row per qualifying final.

## Paragraphs from documents

Every document source reduces the same way: segment the markdown, keep
prose paragraphs over the word floor.
[`doc_paras`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#doc_paras)
is that reduction, and each later fetcher wraps it around one source.
The ref carries the paragraph’s offset, leading back to its place in the
document.
[`readme_paras`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#readme_paras)
reads the AnswerDotAI org through the GitHub GraphQL API, batching the
README fetches into a few requests. It keeps a repo only when it
predates June 2025 (the org’s READMEs are trusted human prose before
that date, and AI-assisted afterwards) and is also checked out in the
local workspace, which restricts the org’s hundreds of repos to a few
dozen libraries.

## The user’s own requests

Long typed prompts are in-medium negatives: chat text, same topics,
human-authored. Two filters guard the label. Prompts carrying harness
markers (hook feedback, command output) were not typed and are skipped.
Prompts pasted from AI output are indistinguishable by marker, and the
low-density cut in
[`build_corpus`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#build_corpus)
is what excludes them.

## READMEs from other people, before ChatGPT

Style diversity on the negative side needs authors other than one
person. `GH_REPOS` is a judgment call, not a search result: from the 250
most-starred pre-2021 repos, the maintained software projects whose
documentation is real English prose, dropping link catalogs, study
guides, interview collections, and non-English content. For each, the
fetcher takes the README as it stood at the cutoff date. Text written
before November 2022 cannot have been written by a chat model, and
mid-2022 leaves comfortable margin. The density cut still applies to
every admitted paragraph. Repos whose org rejects ordinary personal
tokens (a 403) are left off the list.

## Wikipedia, twice

Ordinary Wikipedia supplies competent encyclopedic prose. Simple English
Wikipedia supplies the plainest register in any large corpus: short
sentences, common words, written under rules close to the ones the meter
enforces. Both fetchers take random article intros through the MediaWiki
API.
[`wiki_pair`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#wiki_pair)
fetches the same title from both wikis, giving matched-content pairs
that differ only in register.

## The evaluation labels

The only meter-independent truth is the user’s recorded dissatisfaction:
a `;` prompt, or a complaint about clarity.
[`complaint_labels`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#complaint_labels)
finds those prompts and pairs each with the reply final it reacted to,
which is the previous reply in the same session. Training never reads
these rows. They exist to answer one question: does a scorer rank them
above background? The phrase match over-fires, and every hit was read by
hand: `CL_SKIP` holds the ids judged false, complaints about code or
tests, requests for new work, and rows from testing the hook itself. New
hits join the set only after the same reading.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/slopometer/blob/main/slopometer/corpus.py#L190"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

## Assembly

[`build_corpus`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#build_corpus)
fetches every source, scores each row with
[`label_density`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/corpus.html#label_density),
applies the cuts, and writes two files under XDG state: `corpus.jsonl`
for training and `eval.jsonl` for the complaint labels, which training
must never read. The middle band joins neither side. Measured on this
machine, reply densities run 31/64/124 at the 10th/50th/90th percentile,
and the human sources run far lower but not at zero: your own long
requests reach a median of 37, because genuine questions and dash habits
fire rules there too. The default cuts come from those distributions and
from reading rows at the boundaries: 50 admits seven in ten replies as
confident slop, and 30 admits about half of the human paragraphs. Rows
carry source, ref, and density, so an experiment can re-cut without
refetching.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/slopometer/blob/main/slopometer/corpus.py#L214"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### build_corpus

``` python
async def build_corpus(
    pos_cut:int=50, # Label density at or above which a reply counts as slop
    neg_cut:int=30, # Label density at or below which a human paragraph counts as clean
    wiki_n:int=150, # Random articles per wiki
    out:NoneType=None, # Output directory; default under XDG state
):
```

*Fetch every source, apply the density cuts, and write `corpus.jsonl`
and `eval.jsonl`*

``` python
counts = await build_corpus()
counts
```

Run on this machine, the build wrote 4,540 training rows: 3,417 slop
from replies, and 1,123 clean split 764 requests, 184 curated-repo
README paragraphs, 63 English and 62 Simple English Wikipedia
paragraphs, and 50 workspace README paragraphs. The imbalance is roughly
three to one. Re-cutting needs no refetch, because every row carries its
density. `eval.jsonl` holds the complaint rows.
